source.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
source.authors: Neel Nanda; Lawrence Chan; Tom Lieberum; J. Smith; Jacob Steinhardt

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests grokking on modular addition and uses mechanistic progress measures to track the generalizing circuit. Its analysis differs from simply measuring the original train/test grokking curves.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own modular-addition training runs, mechanistic measurements, ablations, and reported data/weight-decay sweeps. Discussion of other studies’ results is not recorded as rows. The paper also reports many additional architectural and regularization conditions; omitted repeated results are noted below.
record.test_reason: The paper trains small transformers on modular addition, reverse-engineers the learned algorithm, and tracks progress measures through grokking. It is itself a listed original source of the claim (and the origin of V2), so no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that restricted and excluded loss improve continuously before the test-loss drop. The drop occurs during cleanup, after the circuit forms. The authors state that both regularization and limited data are necessary for grokking in their setting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small transformers trained on modular addition with weight decay, as in the original grokking setup, but adds mechanistic reverse engineering, Fourier ablations, and progress measures. The paper also varies architecture, data fraction, modulus, and regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: Grokking depends on training fraction, modulus, and weight decay. Smaller training fractions can delay generalization or prevent it within 40k epochs; ≥ 60% data at P = 113 leads to immediate generalization. The P = 53 outcome changes with weight decay, and P = 401 generalizes immediately across the tested weight decays at 30% data. Key Fourier frequencies vary by seed.
record.problems: The mechanistic analysis and progress measures are specific to small transformers and modular addition. Several curve values are presented only in figures; some settings have few runs or one seed shown. The authors state that their evidence about the intuitive explanation is suggestive and that they lack a general way to predict the phase-transition threshold.
record.rows_left_out: Not every repeated architecture, seed, and regularization result is separately transcribed. Omitted material includes additional per-seed loss/Gini plots in Appendix C.2.1; the full per-model Fourier-fit statistics in Table 5; detailed dropout and L1 sweeps in Appendix D.1; and additional algorithmic-task grokking plots in Appendix D.3. The kept rows cover each tested version and the principal boundary conditions.

untested.parts: No image, text or molecule data; no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich manipulation.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No ungrokking experiment and no critical-dataset-size estimate. The authors say they cannot predict the transition threshold.
Softmax floating-point limits are not tested as a cause of the delay.

missing.what: Reducing loss-calculation precision induced slingshots in a 1-layer model. This bears on numerical and optimizer artifacts (V7).

Grokking appears on 5-digit addition, repeated subsequence and skip-trigram tasks with limited data but not with infinite data. It is declared in rows_left_out but needed to compare V1 across algorithmic tasks.
Dropout p=0.2/0.5 groks on all three seeds; L1 regularization never groks. This bears on whether any low-norm bias suffices for V5.
P=109 behaved exactly like the mainline model.

record.verdict_notes: This study is an original source (arXiv:2301.05217), so no verdict labels are assigned. The text in Appendix D.1 contradicts itself on weight-decay timing; see r19 and r21. r16 says restricted loss declines 'prior to train loss'; this likely means test loss, as in Fig 18. The tranche is set relative to Power et al.: the same task, with a mechanistic method added.

versions.untested_parts: Tests small transformers on modular addition, including how data fraction affects generalization timing. It does not test whether the same timing pattern holds across algorithmic tasks in general.
Tests the Fourier multiplication circuit and restricted/excluded loss progress measures in modular addition. It does not establish that this mechanism applies to other tasks or models.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule setting; no initialization-scale or lazy-to-rich transition test.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning experiment.
Tests weight decay, other regularizers, and data-fraction effects. It does not directly establish a critical dataset-size law or test the proposed ungrokking prediction below a critical size.
Compares the learned algorithm across seeds and several model settings. It does not establish that all architectures and hyperparameters converge to an identical circuit.

Reports that grokking can occur without slingshot behavior, and discusses slingshots and numerical precision. It does not directly test softmax floating-point limits or rule out adaptive-optimizer and numerical artifacts generally.

rows.subject: one-layer ReLU transformer (mainline model)
rows.size_stated: d = 128; 4 attention heads of dimension 32; n = 512 hidden units in the MLP
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch AdamW training on modular addition
rows.measure: Train and test accuracy/loss over training
rows.value: Train accuracy quickly converges to 100%; test accuracy remains low initially and increases to near 100% after around 10,000 epochs.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 shows 5 random seeds; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes early overfitting followed by late generalization.

rows.subject: 1-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the fraction of modular-addition examples used for training
rows.measure: Train and test loss; occurrence of grokking
rows.baseline: Train loss approximately the same across data fractions
rows.value: 10% and 20% of the data did not lead to grokking even after 40k epochs.
rows.note: The paper states these runs overfit and did not generalize within the reported training duration.
rows.check: Runs stopped at 40k epochs with no generalization. This fits a delay growing beyond the horizon, but cannot separate 'never' from 'later'. 'Absent' overstates it for V1.

rows.subject: 1-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the fraction of modular-addition examples used for training
rows.measure: Train and test loss; occurrence and timing of grokking
rows.baseline: Train loss immediately converges to below 10−6 for the fractions plotted in Figure 21.
rows.value: Grokking occurs when between 30 − 50% of the dataset is used; lower fractions lead to slower grokking.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 21 reports steps to loss below 10−6; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The paper says generalization takes significantly longer with lower fractions of data.

source_check.correct: V1: observed. V5: cannot_determine from this row; training-fraction-dependent timing does not establish circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V1, but the timing measurement does not establish the linked V5 efficiency account.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer (mainline model)
rows.size_stated: d = 128; 4 attention heads of dimension 32; n = 512 hidden units in the MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared weight complexity of memorizing and generalizing solutions
rows.measure: Weight norm and loss
rows.value: The authors argue that the completed Fourier multiplication circuit solves the task well and has lower weight than the memorization circuit; weight decay then favors shedding the memorized solution.
rows.uncertainty: The authors present this as an interpretation of their results.
rows.note: This supports the proposed low-norm account in the studied task but is not a direct test of a general critical dataset-size prediction.
rows.check: This is the authors' interpretation (lower-weight circuit favoured by weight decay), not a measured comparison of circuit norms. It should not be a result row; r14 carries the measured weight-norm trajectory.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer (mainline model)
rows.size_stated: d = 128; 4 attention heads of dimension 32; n = 512 hidden units in the MLP
rows.operation_detail: Reverse-engineered weights and activations and tested Fourier-space ablations
rows.measure: Identifiable algorithm underlying modular addition
rows.value: The model uses Fourier multiplication: it represents addition through sine and cosine components at five key frequencies.
rows.note: The paper identifies key frequencies k ∈ {14, 35, 41, 42, 52} for this run.

source_check.correct: The mainline model implements Fourier multiplication using frequencies {14, 35, 41, 42, 52}. For V6, this single-run measurement has state cannot_determine; comparisons across runs are supplied separately in Appendix C.2.
source_check.problem: Identifying one model's algorithm does not by itself establish convergence to the same algorithm across runs.

rows.subject: four other 1-layer transformer runs (random seeds)
rows.size_stated: same architecture as the mainline model
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed embeddings, neuron-logit maps, and projected MLP activations
rows.measure: Whether runs implement the same algorithm
rows.value: All four runs are reported to use the Fourier multiplication algorithm, with different key frequencies across runs.
rows.note: The shared algorithm is a variant of modular arithmetic via Fourier components; the specific frequencies vary by seed.
rows.check: The same algorithm family is used, but key frequencies and their number (3-4 vs 5) differ by seed. Whether this counts as 'the same identifiable algorithm' depends on granularity.

rows.subject: small transformers that generalize correctly in Appendix C.2.2 and D.1
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed learned Fourier components and their contributions to logits

conditions.value: varied data fractions, depth, prime moduli, and regularization

rows.measure: Whether generalizing models use Fourier multiplication
rows.value: The paper states that every model trained with weight decay that generalizes correctly implements some variation of Fourier multiplication.
rows.uncertainty: Table 5 gives model-specific values; no aggregate uncertainty stated.
rows.note: The learned frequencies and degree of fit vary across the reported settings.
rows.check: All generalizing weight-decay models use a Fourier-multiplication variant, but key frequencies differ. Dropout models are not Fourier-sparse (Gini(WE) ≈0.2), and the p=0.2 logit FVE is ~71-74%. Same family, not an identical algorithm.

rows.subject: 1-layer transformers
rows.operation_detail: Compared grokking with the presence of slingshot behavior
rows.measure: Grokking when slingshot behavior is absent
rows.value: Many 1-layer models do not exhibit slingshots but nonetheless grok; the paper concludes the slingshot mechanism is unnecessary for grokking in the presence of regularization.
rows.note: This bears on the proposed adaptive-optimizer artifact explanation, but does not rule out all optimizer or numerical effects.
rows.check: V7 says the delay is an optimizer artifact that disappears when controlled. Many 1-layer models grok without slingshots, so the artifact explanation is absent here, not 'observed'.

relation.reason: The study directly measures delayed generalization and tests its proposed mechanisms across training conditions.

tranche.reason: Mechanistic reverse engineering, Fourier ablations, and progress measures investigate the dynamics underlying grokking.
